title: Rust — Ownership, Traits & Concurrency
description: Core Rust: ownership and borrowing, error handling, dispatch, smart pointers, and the Send/Sync thread-safety markers.

questions.prompt: Rust's borrow checker permits, at any one time, either:

options: Any number of shared (&) references, OR exactly one mutable (&mut) reference
One shared and one mutable reference simultaneously

questions.explanation: Aliasing XOR mutability: many readers or one writer, never both — this is what rules out data races at compile time.

questions.prompt: Assigning a non-Copy value to a new binding moves it, leaving the original binding invalid.
questions.explanation: Move semantics transfer ownership; using the moved-from binding is a compile error unless the type is Copy.

questions.prompt: `dyn Trait` and generic `T: Trait` differ in dispatch as:

options: dyn = dynamic dispatch (vtable); generics = static dispatch (monomorphized)
dyn = static dispatch; generics = dynamic dispatch

questions.explanation: Trait objects dispatch through a vtable at runtime; generics monomorphize to concrete code at compile time.

questions.prompt: Idiomatic Rust models a recoverable error as:
questions.explanation: Result<T, E> makes fallibility explicit in the type; panic! is for unrecoverable bugs.

questions.prompt: Which operator propagates an error early by returning it from the current function?
questions.explanation: The `?` operator returns the Err (or unwraps Ok), converting the error via From.

questions.prompt: To share ownership of a value across threads with reference counting, use:
questions.explanation: Arc is the atomically reference-counted (thread-safe) pointer; Rc is single-threaded only.

questions.prompt: A type that is safe to transfer ownership of to another thread is:
questions.explanation: Send = safe to move across threads; Sync = safe to share &T across threads.

questions.prompt: Iterator adaptors like map and filter are lazy and do no work until the iterator is consumed.
questions.explanation: Nothing runs until a consuming adaptor (collect, sum, for) pulls items through the chain.

questions.prompt: Write `fn sum(v: &[i32]) -> i32` returning the sum of the slice.
questions.explanation: Iterate by reference and use the Sum adaptor. Graded manually.

questions.prompt: Explain how Rust prevents data races at compile time, referencing ownership, borrowing rules, and the Send/Sync traits.

payload.rubric: Connects aliasing-XOR-mutability to race-freedom; notes Send/Sync gate cross-thread sharing; bonus for how Mutex<T> + Arc re-enable shared mutation safely.
